This feature is exposed to superusers and global-access members, so it is a crash path in new code, not an optimization.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate by a datetime key, which is the only way the audit-log endpoint uses it

The audit-log endpoint passes `order_by="-datetime"`. `get_item_key` calls `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on `getattr(item, "datetime")`, which is a `datetime`, so it raises `TypeError` as soon as `build_cursor` computes the next/prev cursor. `value_from_cursor` also returns `cursor.value` as a raw integer instead of converting it back to a datetime, as `DateTimePaginator` does. Any request with a non-zero cursor would therefore compare the `datetime` column to an integer in SQL. The `?optimized_pagination=true` path is broken on the first page and on every later page. The class apparently copies `Paginator` instead of `DateTimePaginator` and was never exercised.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`organization_context.member` dereferenced eagerly for every request, can raise AttributeError on the default path

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated for every request, even when `optimized_pagination` is not set. `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is Optional. It is `None` for non-member access, such as org-auth-token requests where `request.user` is anonymous and `is_superuser` is False. Those requests now fail with `AttributeError` (500) on an endpoint that previously worked. The check should be computed only when `use_optimized` is true, and it should guard against `member is None`.

false_positives.candidate:
Clamping negative offsets in the shared BasePaginator makes cursors inconsistent for all paginators

`BasePaginator.get_result` is inherited by many endpoints. The change silently clamps a negative offset to 0 for the query, but `build_cursor` still receives the original cursor with the negative offset. `_build_next_values` and `_build_prev_values` compute `next_offset = offset + limit` from that negative value. The returned page therefore does not match the cursors that follow it, causing skipped or duplicated rows. Previously a negative offset failed loudly in Django. The comment "the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions" is incorrect, and `is_prev` cursors still pass the negative offset straight through to the slice. This behavior change to a shared class has nothing to do with the spans buffer.

Comment claims Cursor allows negative offsets for reverse pagination, but nothing implements or supports that

The added comment says negative offsets are allowed for "efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions", yet no code changed. `int(offset)` already accepted negatives, and downstream consumers (Django slicing, `build_cursor`) do not support them. The comment misleads future readers into thinking negative offsets are a supported, safe feature.

No test covers the new eviction behavior or the new paginator/endpoint code

The PR's headline feature is evicting spans beyond 1000 per segment inside the Lua script (`zpopmin` on lowest score), and its correctness depends on the score ordering and the union count logic. The tests only add `end_timestamp_precise` to existing fixtures. There is no test that inserts more than 1000 spans and checks which ones survive, or that eviction works across merged sub-segments. There are also no tests for `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, the `optimized_pagination` endpoint path, or the BasePaginator offset clamping. The datetime-key bug and the member-None bug would have been caught by even a basic test.

Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced 10x and explanatory comment removed

The loop bound changes from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the limit is deleted. This is unrelated to the eviction work in the PR. Span trees whose redirect chains are deeper than 1000 will now stop resolving early and fail to merge into the correct segment. That produces split segments, and it is not mentioned in the title or description.

Switching segment storage from Redis SET to ZSET with no migration will hit WRONGTYPE on existing keys

Segment keys `span-buf:s:*` change from sets (`SADD`/`SSCAN`/`SCARD`/`SUNIONSTORE`) to sorted sets (`ZADD`/`ZSCAN`/`ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE`). On deploy, buffers already in Redis are still plain sets, with TTL up to `redis_ttl` (1h). `ZADD`, `ZCARD`, `ZUNIONSTORE` and `ZSCAN` on them will return WRONGTYPE. This causes consumer errors, and flushes of in-flight segments will fail. Nothing handles or documents the transition, such as a new key prefix or draining first.

ZUNIONSTORE uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting scores of duplicate members

Scores are `end_timestamp_precise`, and the eviction via `zpopmin` relies on them as an ordering. `ZUNIONSTORE` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`, so a payload that exists in both `set_key` and `span_key` (or `parent_key`) gets its score doubled. A span redelivered after a consumer restart is one such case. The span then looks far newer than it is, so ordering is wrong and the wrong spans are evicted. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or `MIN`).

max_segment_spans is now dead config and the cap is hard-coded to a different value in Lua

The span-count check in `_load_segment_data` was removed, but `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is still a constructor argument and attribute and is now unused. The real cap is the hard-coded `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`, which does not match the 1001 default and cannot be configured. Eviction also discards the oldest spans without emitting any metric or log, so operators can no longer see that segments are being truncated. The old `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric is gone.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses the outer `dataset` and the raw request query, not the dataset and query actually being executed

`_get_event_stats` receives `scoped_dataset` and `query`, but the eligibility check passes the closure variable `dataset` and `_is_error_focused_query` re-reads `request.GET['query']`. In the dashboard-widget split flow the function is called with `discover` and a derived query such as `(q) AND !event.type:transaction`, and also with the original dataset and query. The decision then reflects neither the dataset nor the query of the call being made. Error-only split queries are not upsampled unless the user's raw query happens to contain `event.type:error`. A transactions or metrics query can be judged eligible because of the outer dataset. The decision should be based on `scoped_dataset` and the `query` argument.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

false_positives.candidate:
Comments claim caching, separation and "current schema assumptions" that the code does not implement

The comments say "This cached result ensures consistent behavior across query execution", "This separation allows for better query optimization and caching" and "ensure we use the most current schema assumptions". The check runs on every call, `upsampling_enabled = should_upsample` is a pure alias, and the "late transformation" is just a list rewrite. The same transform block is also copy-pasted into three branches. The comments mislead readers about the behavior and should be removed, and the transform done once.

Eligibility cache is stale for 60s and its invalidation function is never called

The result of the allowlist check is cached for 60s under a key built only from org id and project ids, not from the allowlist contents. After an operator changes `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, queries keep using the old decision for up to a minute. `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is documented as the fix but has no callers, so it is dead code. The `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` docstring says the config is read "fresh each time" to have the latest state, which contradicts the cache. The key also uses `hash(tuple(...))`, so two project sets can collide and get each other's cached answer; joining the sorted ids would be collision-free.

No tests for the eligibility entry point, the cache, or invalidation

The unit tests cover only the private helpers. `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`, the cache hit/miss paths and `invalidate_upsampling_cache` are never exercised, and nothing checks that an allowlist change is picked up. Negated or OR-combined `event.type` queries and the topEvents path are not tested either. The `snuba_params` built in `setUp` is never used. The endpoint tests mock `options` but not the cache, so they depend on cache state between runs.

Stray submodule gitlink committed

The PR adds a `sentry-repo` entry as a gitlink (`Subproject commit a5d29095...`, the base commit of this very repo) with no matching `.gitmodules`. It is unrelated to the feature and almost certainly an accident. It leaves a dangling submodule entry that makes `git submodule` commands error and confuses checkouts and CI. It should be removed from the PR.

Substring match on `event.type:error` misclassifies queries

`"event.type:error" in query` is a raw substring test on the lowercased query string. It is also true for `!event.type:error` (errors excluded), for `event.type:error OR event.type:transaction` (transactions have no `sample_weight`), and for values like `event.type:error_foo`. Those queries get `count()` rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)`, producing wrong numbers or failing on transaction rows. Parse the query, or at least check for the negation and OR cases.

The "performance" cache adds a cache round trip for something that is already cheap

`options.get` is served from Sentry's local option cache, and the allowlist check is a few integer lookups. Wrapping it in `cache.get`/`cache.set` adds a network round trip (memcached/redis) on every `_get_event_stats` call, and the dashboard split path calls that function several times per request. The dataset and query check, which is the cheap part, runs after the cache access, so even spans, transactions and metrics requests pay for the lookup. The cache costs more than it saves. Evaluating `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform` first and dropping the cache would be simpler and faster.

Upsampled count ignores NULL sample_weight, so events without a sample rate count as 0

`count()` is rewritten to `upsampled_count()`, which is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. Only events that carry a client sample rate get a `sample_weight`. Events in allowlisted projects that predate rollout, or come from SDKs that don't send `client_sample_rate`, have NULL there. `sum` skips NULLs, so those events add 0 and the chart undercounts, possibly showing 0 for projects that do have errors. The comments ("rely on the database schema to ensure sample_weight exists") assert a guarantee nothing in the PR enforces. The aggregate should treat missing weights as 1, for example `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`.

`upsampled_count` is a public discover function not restricted to error data

The new `upsampled_count` SnQLFunction is registered without `private=True`, so any caller of the events or stats API can request `upsampled_count()` directly. On transactions, spans or any non-error query this references a `sample_weight` column that does not exist, so users get Snuba errors or a 500 instead of a validation error. It is also not gated on the allowlist. The function is an internal rewrite target and should be private, like the neighbouring internal function.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
zip(error_ids, events.values()) can pair IDs with the wrong events

`nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` returns a dict keyed by node id. Depending on the backend, it may omit missing keys or not preserve request order. Zipping `error_ids` with `events.values()` can then attach the wrong event id to an event, or shift the pairing after a missing node. Iterate over the `node_ids` and look each one up in the returned dict, or build the id mapping explicitly.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Flagged TableWidgetVisualization renders hard-coded empty data

When `use-table-widget-visualization` is enabled, the table widget passes `columns={[]}` and `tableData={{data: [], meta: {fields: {}, units: {}}}}`. The real `result.data`, `result.meta`, loading state and custom renderers are all ignored. Any org with the flag on sees every dashboard table widget render as an empty grid. Either wire the real query results into the new component or do not ship the branch until it is ready.

true_positives.golden_comment: Validation logic incorrectly uses .get('timestamp'), which treats a timestamp of 0 as absent. It should directly check 'timestamp' in self.initial_data to ensure proper field presence detection, preventing both 'age=0' and 'timestamp' from passing mutual-exclusion validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
age/timestamp exclusivity check uses truthiness and does not require either field

`validate_timestamp` and `validate_age` test `self.initial_data.get("age")` and `get("timestamp")` for truthiness. A report with `age: 0` or `timestamp: 0` (both valid) passes alongside the other field, so the 'mixed' check is bypassed. Both fields are also `required=False`, and field-level validators only run when the field is present. A report with neither `age` nor `timestamp` is accepted even though one of them is mandatory. The docstrings also describe the opposite of what the code checks. Use `is not None` checks and add object-level validation that exactly one of the two is present.

true_positives.golden_comment: Analytics events are recorded before the feature flag check, resulting in analytics being logged for all requests, including those that return 404 due to the feature being disabled. This can lead to misleading analytics data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Analytics event recorded before the feature-flag check

`analytics.record("preprod_artifact.api.assemble", ...)` fires before the `organizations:preprod-artifact-assemble` feature check and before any payload validation. Requests from organizations without the feature, which get a 404, still emit the event. That inflates usage numbers for a feature that is not enabled. Move the call after the feature gate, or after validation, so only real attempts are counted.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The BrowserReportingCollectorEndpoint returns HttpResponse objects but the endpoint inherits from Endpoint which expects rest_framework.response.Response objects.
In BaseDetectorTypeValidator.update(), the validator incorrectly updates instance.type using validated_data.get('detector_type') instead of validated_data.get('type').

false_positives.candidate:
60s processing deadline may be too short for a 100-identity chunk

`check_auth_identities` loops over up to `chunk_size=100` identities. Each one runs `check_single_auth_identity`, which can call the SSO provider's `refresh_identity` over the network. A 60s deadline can be exceeded when providers are slow. Those identities already had `last_synced` bumped in `check_auth` before scheduling, so a timed-out chunk is not rechecked until the next interval. The follow-up `check_auth.apply_async` at the end of the task also never runs for that chunk.

Default autofix automation tuning silently changed from 'low' to 'off'

`DEFAULT_AUTOFIX_AUTOMATION_TUNING_DEFAULT` and the `sentry:autofix_automation_tuning` project option default (src/sentry/projectoptions/defaults.py) both flip from `low` to `off`. Every project that never set the option changes behavior on deploy: automatic autofix on new issues stops. The change is unrelated to the PR's stated purpose (replay bulk delete) and has no description or migration plan. Confirm it is intended and split it out so it can be rolled out and reverted independently.

Error timestamps (seconds) are compared against replay event timestamps (milliseconds)

`gen_request_data` compares `error_events[i]["timestamp"]` with `event.get("timestamp", 0)`. Error timestamps come from the nodestore event payload and are float seconds (~1.7e9). Replay recording events (rrweb) carry millisecond timestamps (~1.7e12). Every error is therefore treated as earlier than the first replay event, and all errors are emitted at the start of the log instead of interleaved chronologically. The unit tests hide this because they use seconds for both sides (`now.timestamp()`, 1.5/3.0). The error timestamp should be converted to ms, or the replay timestamp to seconds, before comparing and before formatting the log line.

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES only applied when a search query is entered

`HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` (`is_segment`, `project_id`, `received`) is checked only in the `.filter()` that runs after the `if (!searchQuery.trim()) return sorted;` early return. With an empty search box, which is the default, the hidden attributes are still shown. They disappear as soon as the user types something, so the list changes inconsistently. The hidden-attribute filter needs to run before the early return so it applies in both cases.

None max_segment_id handling is not exercised by any test

The new early return for `max_segment_id is None` in `_make_recording_filenames` is only reached through `test_run_bulk_replay_delete_job_completion`, which patches `delete_matched_rows`. The real filename generation and deletion therefore never runs with a null segment id. Add a direct unit test for `_make_recording_filenames` / `delete_matched_rows` with a `None` row so a regression would be caught.

Query key omits organization slug

The key is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`, but `queryFn` fetches `/organizations/${organization.slug}/trace-items/attributes/` via `useGetTraceItemAttributeKeys`. The org slug is not part of the key. Switching organizations with otherwise identical page filters, project ids and item type can serve cached attributes from the wrong org. Include `organization.slug` in the key.

Snuba replay query runs even when error context is disabled

`query_replay_instance` and `process_raw_response` are executed unconditionally to obtain `error_ids`. The `enable_error_context=false` check is only evaluated afterwards, so the result is discarded. A disabled request still pays for an extra Snuba query. Check the flag first and skip the query.

Strict ChoiceField for report type rejects the whole batch with 422

The old dataclass did not enforce the `Literal` type at runtime. `type = ChoiceField(choices=BROWSER_REPORT_TYPES)` now returns 422 for the entire request if any report has a type outside the eight hard-coded values, such as other Reporting API types browsers may send. The endpoint is explicitly meant to collect real-world data on what browsers send. One unknown report therefore drops every valid report in the same POST and discards the data the experiment is trying to observe. Consider accepting unknown types (tagging them as 'unknown' in the metric) and validating per report rather than failing the whole batch.

get_environment_info does a per-issue event lookup and logs failures as info

For each issue in the PR comment, `get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()`, which can hit Snuba and nodestore. That is up to five extra lookups, executed serially in the list comprehension while building the comment. Any exception is swallowed and logged at `info` under the name `no-environment`. Real failures such as Snuba errors are indistinguishable from 'issue has no environment' and will not alert. Consider batching or using data already available from the query, and log failures at a higher level.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write

The codes are decrypted, the matching entry is set to null, and the whole array is re-encrypted and written back, with no transaction or compare-and-set. Two concurrent logins with the same code can both read it as unused and both succeed, so 'usable exactly once' is not guaranteed. Concurrent consumption of two different codes can also overwrite each other. The second write restores the code the first request just burned. An atomic update guarded on the previous ciphertext value, or a transaction with row locking, would fix this.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup codes and blob URL are never cleared or revoked when the modal closes

`resetState` only resets the password, error message and step. The plaintext `backupCodes`, `secret` and `dataUri` stay in component state, and the Blob object URL created in `handleSetup` is only revoked if setup is run again. It is not revoked on close or unmount. The sensitive codes therefore stay in memory and the blob URL leaks for the life of the page. Clear this state in `resetState` and revoke the URL in cleanup.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup-code login can skip the password check by sending a dummy totpCode

The password is only verified when `!credentials.totpCode` (line 121). The new `user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode` branch runs before any TOTP validation and never looks at `totpCode`. A request with `email`, a bogus non-empty `totpCode` (e.g. "000000") and a valid `backupCode` skips password verification and then authenticates on the backup code alone. Before this PR a bogus `totpCode` failed the TOTP check. Now it does not, because the backup branch short-circuits it. Backup codes are static, long-lived secrets, so this makes them a standalone credential that replaces the password. The backup branch should verify the password itself, or the password skip should be conditioned on a TOTP code that is actually validated.

Copy button shows success toast without awaiting clipboard write

`navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` returns a promise that rejects on permission denial or in non-secure contexts. It is neither awaited nor caught, and the 'Backup codes copied!' toast is shown unconditionally. A user can believe the codes were copied when they were not, and the codes cannot be retrieved again afterwards.

Dismissing the dialog on the backup-codes step skips onEnable/resetState

After a successful enable, the modal moves to `DisplayBackupCodes` and hides the Cancel button. The dialog is still dismissable through `onOpenChange` (Escape or clicking the overlay). That path calls neither `onEnable()` nor `resetState()`. The parent is not told 2FA is now enabled, so the settings switch can stay stale until a reload. When the modal is reopened the component may still be on the backup-codes step with the old codes. Backup codes cannot be shown again, so a user who dismisses by accident can lose them. The close handler should route through the same cleanup as the Close button, or the dialog should not be dismissable on this step.

No tests for the actual backup-code behavior; first e2e test left on backup-code screen

The new logic is not covered: login with a backup code, single-use enforcement, wrong or missing codes, and disabling 2FA with a backup code. The TODO on line 12 admits this. The 'enable and login' test never closes the new backup-codes dialog, and its `expect(locator.isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` assertion is vacuous because it asserts on a Promise (acknowledged by the new FIXME). The security-sensitive server paths in `authorize` and `disable.ts` have no automated coverage.

Unrelated change removes the password show/hide toggle from keyboard navigation globally

Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the toggle inside the shared `PasswordField` affects every password field in the app. Keyboard and screen-reader users can no longer tab to the show/hide button, an accessibility regression unrelated to backup codes. Nothing in this feature requires it, so it should be scoped to the places that need it or dropped.

The PR changes the cancellation contract: `cancelled` flag, lazy vs. immediate delete, and the cron cancelling reminders within the next hour. It adds no tests. The whole loop is inside a single try/catch, and the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete` calls are lazy Prisma promises that only execute at the final `Promise.all`. If one `client.request` throws (invalid or expired batch_id, rate limit, transient error), the loop exits. No row is deleted, including those already cancelled in SendGrid. The next cron run fetches the same rows in the same order and hits the same failing reminder first. That one bad row then stops every reminder after it from being cancelled, so those emails are still sent. Wrap each reminder in its own try/catch, and delete or mark each row right after its own successful cancel.

`Prisma` is now an unused value import

The import was changed from `import type { Prisma, PrismaPromise }` to a value import that also pulls in `Prisma`. After removing the `Prisma.BatchPayload` usage, `Prisma` is no longer referenced anywhere in the file, so it will trigger an unused-import lint warning. The same edit left a missing trailing comma. In the commented-out `testAction` block the diff also strips indentation, which is pure noise.

Only `sgMail.setApiKey` is called here. `@sendgrid/mail` keeps its own client instance, whereas the default export of `@sendgrid/client` is a separate singleton. The new cancel loop now depends on `client.request` for `/v3/user/scheduled_sends`. If the singleton has no key in this process, every cancel fails with 401. The surrounding try/catch swallows that with a console.log, and nothing is cancelled. Call `client.setApiKey(sendgridAPIKey)` in this file.

The `forEach` callbacks call `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder` without awaiting them. Every entry is `import("./app")`, evaluated when the `appStore` object literal is created. The first file that imports `@calcom/app-store` therefore starts loading all ~29 app packages, including their heavy SDKs and module-level side effects. true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`end` in the working-hours check is computed from the slot start, not the slot end

`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is identical to `start`, so `end > workingHour.endTime` only tests the slot's start. A slot that starts inside working hours but runs past the end (for example a 60-minute slot at 16:30 with working hours ending at 17:00) is treated as available. It should use `slotEndTime` (start plus event length).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with `===` so the zero-length override branch never fires

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two freshly created object references, which is always false, so this branch is dead code. The intent was to detect a zero-length (fully unavailable) override. Use `.isSame(...)` or compare `valueOf()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override early return skips the busy-time check, allowing double bookings

When a slot falls on a day with a date override and is not rejected by the range checks, `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` returns before the `busy.every(...)` block. Bookings, calendar busy times and buffers are therefore never consulted for that host on override days. A fixed host with an override can be offered a slot that overlaps an existing booking or calendar event. This applies to every personal and collective event too, since those hosts are all treated as fixed. The override should only decide whether the slot is inside working time, and the busy check should still run afterwards.

Multiple date overrides on the same day make slots unavailable

The override check uses `find`, which returns true ("slot not within override") if the slot is outside any one override whose day matches. A user can have several override ranges on one date, for example 9-12 and 14-17. A slot at 10:00 is inside the first range but before the second, so the second range returns true and the slot is rejected. A slot is only outside the overrides when it is outside all of them for that day. The check should be an `every`/`some` over the day's overrides, not a short-circuit on the first miss.

Override day compared via server-local formatting against UTC slot day

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` formats in the server's local timezone, but it is compared with `slotStartTime.format(...)`, which is UTC. On any server whose TZ is not UTC (local dev, some deployments) the day match can be off by one and silently apply or skip overrides. Even in UTC, matching on the UTC calendar day rather than the organizer's calendar day misassigns overrides near midnight, for example a 02:00-05:00 IST override that lies on the previous UTC day. Both sides should be formatted in the same explicit timezone, normally the organizer's.

Override day filter and time-of-day wrap are not adjusted for the new timezone offset

The new offset is applied to the override's hour and minute, but `activeOverrides` still picks overrides by comparing the unshifted `override.start` to the invitee's day boundaries. An override can therefore be assigned to the wrong invitee day. Example: organizer wall-clock 20:00 and invitee +6:00. The offset is also applied via `.hour() * 60 + .minute()`, which wraps modulo 24h. An override that shifts across midnight gets a start and end on different days, so `end < start`. `buildSlots` then drops it as invalid or places it on the wrong day. The shifted range needs to be mapped to the correct invitee day and split or clamped at midnight.

Tests do not cover the main fix (fixed-host date overrides) and the new timezone test is weak

The PR's headline fix is that a fixed host's date override restricts round-robin slots. No test creates a round-robin event with a fixed host and an override, and none covers split working hours, multiple overrides per day, or an override day with busy bookings. Those are exactly the cases where the new `checkIfIsAvailable` logic breaks. The added Dhaka test only asserts the same UTC slots as the IST case. The custom `toHaveTimeSlots` matcher iterates only over the actual slots and never checks the length, so missing expected slots would still pass.

Working-hours check rejects slots for any user with several ranges on the same day

`workingHours.find(...)` returns true, meaning "outside working hours", as soon as the slot is outside any single working-hour entry that includes today. `getWorkingHours` yields one entry per distinct start/end range, so a user with 9-12 and 13-17 on Mon-Fri has two entries covering the same days. A slot at 10:00 is inside the first entry but outside the second, so the whole slot is rejected. Because personal and collective hosts are `isFixed`, every user with a split schedule, such as a lunch break, would now lose all their slots. The check must pass if the slot is inside at least one entry (`some`/`every` with the logic inverted), not fail if it is outside any one.

`override.start.toString()` and optional `timeZone` used for offset calculation

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` goes through `Date.toString()`, which is locale and format dependent and drops milliseconds; pass the `Date` directly. `override.timeZone` is optional in the `TimeRange` type, and `.tz(undefined)` falls back to the server's guessed zone. Any caller that does not set `timeZone` silently gets a wrong offset (or zero) instead of the old behaviour. There should be a fallback to `organizerTimeZone` or an explicit skip when it is missing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

`test_basic` begins with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`. The new `time.sleep(0.1)` ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") calls the patched function and does nothing. The test therefore still races: `step.join()` sets `stopped` immediately after the drift change, and the flusher thread may exit before flushing, making `(msg,) = messages` flaky. The extra `step.poll()` doesn't help either. Capture the real sleep before patching, or poll/wait until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process) is False for spawn-context processes, so hung flushers are never killed

Processes are created with `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which is `SpawnProcess`. `SpawnProcess` subclasses `BaseProcess`, not `multiprocessing.context.Process`, which is what `multiprocessing.Process` refers to. So `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is always False for real flusher processes. The original code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally; this PR guards it with that isinstance check, so `kill()` is now dead code. When a flusher is detected as hung, the old process keeps running while `_create_process_for_shards` starts a replacement on the same shards. The result is duplicate flushers on one shard (possible duplicate segments to Kafka), leaked processes, and eventually the MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS crash. The same check in `join()` (around line 346) means `terminate()` is never called either. Check against `multiprocessing.context.BaseProcess`, or use `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched

`test_basic` begins with `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`. The new `time.sleep(0.1)` ("Give flusher threads time to process after drift change") calls the patched function and does nothing. The test therefore still races: `step.join()` sets `stopped` immediately after the drift change, and the flusher thread may exit before flushing, making `(msg,) = messages` flaky. The extra `step.poll()` doesn't help either. Capture the real sleep before patching, or poll/wait until `messages` is non-empty with a timeout.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can break out of the loop and skip waiting for or terminating the remaining processes

In the new per-process join loop, once the deadline expires the code does `break`. This skips the wait and the `terminate()` for all remaining processes. The original code always attempted `terminate()` after the wait. With multiple processes, one slow process can consume the whole timeout and leave the others neither awaited nor terminated. They are only cleaned up if they are daemons and the parent exits. Iterate over all processes and terminate stragglers after the deadline instead of breaking.

false_positives.candidate:
Docstring claims one process per shard, but the number of processes is capped by max_processes

The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing." Actually `num_processes = min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` and shards are distributed round-robin, so processes can serve several shards. The CLI option `--flusher-processes` defaults to 1, so by default a single process handles all shards. The docstring misleads readers and operators about the default behavior.

New test only checks process counts, not distribution, flush behavior or restart logic

`test_flusher_processes_limit` asserts `len(processes)==2` and that the total shard count is 4. It does not check that each shard appears in exactly one process or that spans from different shards are flushed. It also doesn't exercise `_ensure_processes_alive` (restart/kill) or the real spawn path, since it uses the threaded `produce_to_pipe` mode. The restart/kill regression (spawn `Process` not matching the `isinstance` check) therefore goes untested.

No validation of --flusher-processes; negative values crash SpanFlusher

`--flusher-processes` is a plain `int` with no lower bound. `0` silently falls back to one process per shard because of `max_processes or len(shards)`. A negative value makes `num_processes` negative, so `process_to_shards_map` is empty. The distribution loop then does `i % self.num_processes`, which is 0 for `-1` and raises `KeyError` on the empty map. Use `click.IntRange(min=1)`.

Unused `_create_process_for_shard` helper

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called. `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly. This is dead code and should be removed.

submit() now makes per-process Redis calls on every message, with redundant memory-info queries

Before, `submit` called `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()` once on one buffer. Now it iterates all per-process buffers. Each buffer is built over a subset of shards but points at the same Redis cluster(s), so cluster-wide `get_memory_info()` is repeated N times and the results summed. The used/available ratio is unchanged, but Redis INFO round-trips on the consumer's main thread scale with the flusher process count, which defeats the goal of keeping the main thread minimal. Query memory once (e.g. via the main buffer) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and passes only by timing

The docstring says 'errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages', but the test asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. With the actual implementation both offsets (the failing one included) are completed in the worker's `finally` and would be committed by the commit loop after its 1s wait. The assertion passes only because the test checks within about 0.3s, before the first commit tick. It verifies nothing about error handling and will fail or flake if timing changes. It should wait for a commit and assert that offsets 100 and 101 are committed (as 102), or assert the intended behavior explicitly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own daemon thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`. In the factory that wraps arroyo's `commit` callback, which stages offsets on the `KafkaConsumer` and may commit. That state is owned by the `StreamProcessor` thread and is not designed for concurrent access while the main thread is polling, pausing or rebalancing. The loop can also commit offsets for partitions that were just revoked, which raises inside the thread; the exception is swallowed and retried every second. Commits should be driven from `poll()`/`submit()` on the consumer thread, using the tracker's committable offsets, rather than from a separate thread.

Docstring claims offsets are committed only after successful processing

The worker's `finally` block calls `complete_offset` even when `result_processor` raised. Failed items therefore become committable and are committed, so processing errors are skipped rather than retried. The docstring 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' is wrong. Similarly, `terminate()` calls `shutdown()` with `immediate=False`, which does not actually terminate quickly.

Flaky assertions on queue depth and on hash distribution

`test_stats_reporting` asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0` right after submitting 10 items to live worker threads. The workers only append to a list, so they can drain everything before the check. `test_different_groups_distributed` (line 106) asserts that 20 string keys hit all 3 queues. Python string hashes are randomized per process, so this fails for a small fraction of runs (about 0.1%). Both should avoid depending on timing or on the hash seed, for example by blocking the processor on an event or by choosing keys with known assignments.

Gap detection only works until the first commit; later gaps are skipped

`start = max(last_committed + 1, min_offset)` skips any gap between `last_committed` and the smallest tracked offset. `mark_committed` prunes `all_offsets` to offsets above the committed one. With offsets 100, 102, 103 tracked, the first pass commits 100. The next pass sees `all_offsets={102,103}`, `start=102`, and commits 103 without 101 ever being tracked or completed. `test_offset_gaps_block_commits` (and the uptime gaps test) do not catch this: the first one passes because it submits 101 before the second commit can matter, and the other only checks the first commit. The documented guarantee ('only commits when all prior offsets are processed') is not enforced. Contiguity should be checked against `last_committed + 1`, or the tracker should rely on in-order submission explicitly.

Strategy close() shuts down the factory-owned queue pool, so messages are dropped after the first rebalance

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` and the same instance is handed to every `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` from `create_with_partitions`. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the old strategy at each partition revoke. `close()` and `join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown=True`, shuts every queue and joins the workers. The next `create_with_partitions` reuses the dead pool. Its workers have exited and `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` catches that exception, logs it, then calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset`. Every message after the first rebalance is therefore silently dropped and its offset is committed, which is data loss. The shared `OffsetTracker` also keeps stale `last_committed` and `all_offsets` state across assignments. The strategy should not own or shut down the pool (the factory's `shutdown()` should), or the pool must be created per strategy.

Unbounded queues and no MessageRejected, despite the documented 'natural backpressure'

The class docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but each queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `submit` never raises arroyo's `MessageRejected`. If one worker stalls on a slow item, the consumer keeps polling and enqueueing. Memory grows without bound and the backlog is never limited by the poll loop. The offset tracker's `all_offsets` and `outstanding` sets also grow because the stuck offset blocks all later commits. Either bound the queues and reject when full, or remove the claim.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test is vacuous: it would pass without the denial short-circuit

The test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' comments that it allows access to prove the permission cache is not consulted. It sets the permCache value to `false` (`{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`), which does not grant anything. Without the denial-cache logic, `checkPermission` would see no grant and fall through to the empty fake store, so the result is still `Allowed=false`. The test therefore passes whether or not the denial cache works. It should set the scope to `true` and/or use a store that would grant access, so that only the denial entry can produce the deny.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Underscore-joined denial key is ambiguous for names and folders that contain underscores

The key is `ns.perm_<user>_<action>_<name>_<parent>`, joined with `_`. Dashboard and folder UIDs commonly contain underscores, so different (name, folder) pairs can map to the same key. For example, name `a_b` with folder `c` and name `a` with folder `b_c` both produce `..._a_b_c`. A denial for one resource then wrongly denies the other for the TTL. The key also shares the `perm_<user>_<action>` prefix with the permission-map key, which holds a different value type. Use an unambiguous separator or a distinct prefix such as `perm_denied_`, and consider hashing or escaping the components.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Cached denials are not invalidated when permissions are refreshed

A denial entry is written for 30s and consulted before the permission cache. If a user's permissions are refreshed from the DB between the denial and a later check, for example by a check or List on another resource, the permission cache can already grant the resource. The denial entry still takes precedence, so access stays denied until the denial TTL expires. The same applies if a permission is granted after an earlier check on a not-yet-existing resource. This partly defeats the goal of letting a creator access a just-created dashboard or folder. When `getUserPermissions` repopulates the permission cache, the denial entry for the checked resource should be dropped, or the allowed result should be authoritative.

Denial cache key omits identity type, so anonymous and renderer share denials

`userPermDenialCacheKey` is built from `checkReq.UserUID`, the ID part of the subject, and does not include the identity type. `anonymous:0` and `render:0` both yield UserUID `0`, so they get the same denial key for the same namespace, action, name and folder. The denial lookup in `Check` runs before any identity-specific logic. If an anonymous check on `dashboards:read` for `dash1` is denied, the denial is cached for 30s. A renderer check for the same dashboard is then denied from the cache, although the renderer is granted read on all dashboards and folders. The result is renders that fail intermittently for up to the TTL. The key should include the identity type, or the resolved internal UID, as the permission cache keys do.

Every first-time denial for a distinct resource triggers a DB permission re-query

When cached permissions do not allow the request, `Check` always falls through to `getIdentityPermissions`, which queries the DB. The only mitigation is the denial cache, which is keyed per (user, action, name, folder). A user without access to many resources, such as a UI or search path that checks many dashboards individually, therefore causes one permission query per distinct denied resource until each has its own denial entry. Singleflight only deduplicates concurrent calls. This weakens the cache and can amplify load on the SQL permission store, including for unauthorized or probing callers who vary the resource name. Consider rate-limiting the re-query, for example a per-user/action 'recently refreshed' marker, so that a fresh DB fetch is not repeated within a short window.

No test that a DB-derived denial is written to the denial cache; removed cache-hit case leaves dead test fields

The new tests cover reading a pre-seeded denial entry. None checks that `Check` writes a denial entry after a DB-confirmed deny, which is the behaviour that protects the DB from repeated queries. None checks that an allowed result does not write one. Nothing covers the anonymous or renderer paths through the new cache-then-DB flow, or the case where the identity lookup fails. The 'permissions from cache' case was also deleted from `TestService_getUserPermissions`, so the `cacheHit` field is now always false there and effectively dead code.

The component doc says it 'Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints', and the `expectedRulesCount` doc says 'Ruler response might contain different number of rules'. The component no longer calls the Ruler API. Update both comments to avoid misleading future readers.

Tests encode the missing Delete item and miss the broken Silence flow

The test grants `AlertingRuleDelete` and `AlertingRuleUpdate` but asserts exactly four menu items with no Delete. That locks in the regression where Delete and Pause are unreachable from the list view. No test clicks 'Silence notifications' and checks that the drawer opens, which would have caught the dead action.
